newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-AUGUSTA NATIONAL IS EARLY LEADER IN MASTERS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-AUGUSTA NATIONAL IS EARLY LEADER IN MASTERS.

text.p: Birdies were rarer than crabgrass at Augusta National Golf Club on Thursday as the first round of the Masters produced more crashes than an American stock car race.

With double, triple and even quadruple bogeys littering the scoreboard, Paul Azinger managed to break par, shooting three-under 69 for a lead that only a handful of players had a chance of overcoming.
Azinger was two shots clear of Costantino Rocca of Italy, who birdied three of the first four holes on the back nine to shoot a solid 71.

He was one ahead of nine other players at level par, including two-time champion Bernhard Langer of Germany, 1992 champion Fred Couples, 1993 U.S. Open winner Lee Janzen and pre-tournament favourites Davis Love and Briton Colin Montgomerie.
Also matching par on a day when par was a very good score were young Americans David Berganio and Tommy Tolles, and Masters rookies Stuart Appleby of Australia and Per-Ulrik Johansson of Sweden.

Only four players were under par and still a threat to Azinger -- 1994 champion Jose Maria Olazabal of Spain, former British Open and PGA Champion Nick Price of Zimbabwe and Americans Paul Stankowski, John Houston and rookie sensation Tiger Woods.
The 21-year-old Woods was four over after nine holes but he birdied three of the first four holes after the turn to jump into contention in only his third Masters, and first as a professional.
Woods, seeking to become the youngest Masters champion, outplayed defending champion Nick Faldo in the most closely followed pairing of the day.
Faldo, who already owns three green jackets, went out in a shocking five over par but recovered with three birdies in four holes to stand at two over after 15 holes.

Azinger, winner of the 1993 PGA Championship for his only major title, posted his best opening round in 10 Masters despite swirling winds and pin placements so perplexing that players were happy with three putts on some greens.
"It just happened," Azinger said in trying to explain how he managed to make four birdies and only one bogey while all those around him seemed to struggle so mightily.
"The wind was coming out of different directions," he admitted, "and the greens were scary fast."

Azinger, fully recovered from the cancer that sidelined him for most of 1994, used fine iron play to negate what he called "pretty severe" greens. Two of his birdies came on putts of two feet and the others were from six and 12 feet.
"I got more sure of myself putting as the round went on," he said. But he didn't take anything for granted on Augusta's big, undulating greens.
"I had a lot of six-to-10-footers that I was just trying to two-putt," he confessed.
"It was like walking through a battlefield," Janzen said after surviving some of the most difficult playing conditions seen at Augusta in many years.
"It was by far the toughest I've ever seen the course play," added Janzen, making his sixth Masters appearance.
Janzen, like many others, said the combination of swirling winds, lightning-fast greens and some extremely difficult pin positions made pars something to covet.

A club official, in a highly uncharacteristic revelation for Augusta National, said the committee that decided where to cut the holes on the putting surfaces had been taken by surprise by the wind and the firmness of the greens.
"The conditions were more difficult than they thought they would be," the official said.
It was a statement that provoked no argument.
